It fell to Lucius Aemilius Paullus, consul of 168 BC, to bring Perseus finally to a decisive battle. Around sixty years of age, Paullus was a harsh old veteran. As praetor in 191, Paullus had been victorious in Spain. As consul for the first time in 182, he had defeated the Ligurians.

When selected for the Macedonian command, Paullus pointedly refused to thank the Roman people for electing him, scorning the immemorial custom of the Romans. He was doing them a favor by undertaking to finish the war against Perseus, he said, rather than receiving a favor from them.

Then he warned them brusquely against second-guessing him, gossiping about the war, forming ill-informed opinions, and offering useless advice.
